The term "multi-omics integration" is frequently invoked as though it referred to a single statistical operation, yet the algorithmic landscape encompasses fundamentally different commitments to the data-generating process. Methods as superficially similar as similarity-network fusion and matrix factorisation impose distinct assumptions about the distribution of signal across modalities, the nature of cross-platform concordance, and the role of prior biological knowledge, and a working taxonomy is required before any meaningful comparison of software tools can be undertaken. In what follows, I organise the field along three axes: the stage at which integration is performed (early, intermediate or late), the degree of supervision required (unsupervised, semi-supervised or supervised), and the biological target the analysis is designed to address (subtyping, biomarker selection, longitudinal modelling or dynamic network inference).

The most informative first axis is integration stage. Early integration concatenates normalised modality matrices into a single design matrix and applies standard multivariate or supervised methods, an approach implemented, for example, in PLS-based workflows within mixOmics [R3]. Concatenation preserves the original feature space but ignores modality-specific noise structure and is highly sensitive to differences in scale and feature cardinality. Intermediate integration builds a joint latent representation, either by factor-analytic decomposition as in Multi-Omics Factor Analysis [R2], MOTL [R42] and Multi-Layer Matrix Factorisation [R13], or by graph-based embedding as in SNF [R5], MODILM [R52] and MO-GCAN [R39]. Late, or decision-level, integration trains separate models on each modality and combines their outputs; deep learning frameworks such as DeepMoIC [R19] and MOADLN [R23] instantiate intermediate integration through latent representation fusion, with downstream classification heads that yield decision-level outputs. Crucially, these three strategies are not interchangeable: the choice of stage changes the failure modes of an analysis, and tools marketed under a single integration label frequently combine stages internally without disclosing the implications.

The second axis concerns supervision. Unsupervised factor-analytic methods dominate the literature precisely because matched multi-omics cohorts are usually too small to support fully labelled learning; MOFA infers shared and modality-specific latent factors without external labels and then enables downstream subtyping, imputation and outlier detection [R2], while mixOmics provides a continuum from unsupervised PLS variants to the supervised discriminant variant DIABLO [R3, R35]. Semi-supervised approaches explicitly leverage small labelled subsets alongside large unlabelled ones: SSD-MO combines deep non-negative matrix factorisation with a semi-supervised objective and was shown to improve clustering F-scores on six TCGA datasets [R9], although the extent to which these gains generalise beyond cancer subtyping has not been established. Fully supervised frameworks such as the network-based Bayesian method NetMIM [R20] and the graph-attention-based MODILM [R52] address biomarker selection and disease classification directly, but they depend on the existence of trustworthy endpoints and cannot answer exploratory questions about novel molecular strata.

The third axis, biological target, distinguishes tools whose statistical machinery is tailored to a specific scientific goal. Sample subtyping is the most heavily studied target: SNF fuses per-modality patient similarity networks and was reported to outperform single-modality analyses and several integration baselines across five cancer cohorts [R5], while MLMF extends factorisation to handle partial multi-omics matrices across twelve multi-omics datasets drawn from cancer studies [R13], and graph-attention and graph-convolutional approaches such as MO-GCAN [R39] and DeepMoIC [R19] target the same problem with neural architectures. Biomarker selection is the explicit objective of DIABLO [R35] and NetMIM [R20], the latter additionally accommodating block missingness through data augmentation. A more specialised target is longitudinal modelling, addressed by timeOmics [R27] and PALM [R31], with PALM aligning multi-omics time series before reconstructing dynamic Bayesian networks in an inflammatory bowel disease cohort [R31]. Dynamic network inference proper, the reconstruction of time-resolved regulatory graphs spanning omics layers, is the central aim of netOmics [R28] and PALM [R31], and is statistically distinct from subtyping even though both produce graphical outputs.

This three-axis taxonomy should not, however, be read as a neutral classification. The benchmarks available do not yet justify a confident ranking across stages: the single-cell integration benchmark of Hu and colleagues reports that Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI outperform other vertical-integration methods on most of the 47 datasets evaluated [R17], while a parallel benchmark of joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq integration finds that no single method dominates across tasks [R48], and neither study examines bulk multi-omics subtyping or longitudinal targets. Conflating similarity-network fusion with matrix factorisation obscures a real methodological contrast: SNF operates by fusing per-modality sample similarity networks [R5], whereas factor-analytic methods such as MOFA infer a small number of shared and modality-specific latent axes [R2], and empirical benchmarks to date have not formally distinguished these alternative data-generating assumptions. What the literature does not show is that any single axis dominates the others; integrative method choice must therefore be made conditional on the assumed data-generating process, the size and labelling of the cohort, and the specific biological question being asked, and software reviews that ignore these axes risk endorsing tools whose assumptions are violated by the very data they are applied to.

integration frameworks occupy an unusual position in the multi-omics software landscape: they are not tied to a particular biological question or sample type, but instead supply statistical machinery that operates on whatever blocks the user supplies. Within the R/Bioconductor ecosystem, this category is anchored by the MultiAssayExperiment class, which provides a coordinated representation of diverse assays together with subsetting, reshaping and cross-assay aggregation primitives [R36]. MultiAssayExperiment does not enforce any particular model: it is an interchange format on top of which methods such as MOFA, mixOmics or pathway-based routines can be plugged in, and the SingleCellMultiModal Bioconductor package redistributes curated landmark CITE-seq, 10x Multiome and related datasets as MultiAssayExperiment objects to support method development on standardised inputs [R51].

The most visible statistical engines are the PLS-family methods consolidated in mixOmics, which provides sparse and discriminant variants for dimension reduction and feature selection across multiple 'omics blocks [R3]. DIABLO, the supervised extension implemented within the same package, seeks correlated discriminant features across data types and has been adopted for cancer case studies integrating mRNA, miRNA, CpG, protein and metabolite matrices [R35]. PLS-based methods are, by construction, linear and rely on cross-block covariance structure; in highly compositional or sparsity-dominated data, such as sparse microbiome count tables with many zeros and strong library-size effects, this construction can yield unstable loading signs and inflated cross-block correlations, so users are well advised to verify the linearity and correlation assumptions empirically before trusting cross-omics feature signatures. This limitation reflects the underlying PLS methodology rather than any specific shortcoming of the mixOmics implementation, and applies to any PLS-derived integrator rather than to mixOmics in particular.

Factor-analytic frameworks relax the assumption of correlated blocks by learning latent factors that can be shared or modality-specific. MOFA was introduced as an unsupervised probabilistic factor model for bulk multi-omics, providing sample subtyping, imputation and outlier detection [R2]. The single-cell-focused MOFA+ generalised this formulation with scalable inference and flexible sparsity priors to handle multiple sample groups and modalities such as paired RNA and epigenetic profiling [R4]. These models offer probabilistic grounding and factor-level interpretability, but the documented case studies are limited to specific cancer settings [R2]; whether MOFA-style factor inference generalises to the zero-inflated compositional distributions typical of microbiome relative abundance matrices, or how factor interpretability behaves as the number of modalities grows beyond three, remains, to our knowledge, untested in the cited primary literature. Extensions such as MOTL have begun to address limited-sample settings by transferring factor structure from larger datasets [R42], illustrating that active development of the MOFA family continues beyond the original publications and that conclusions drawn from the original MOFA and MOFA+ studies [R2, R4] should not be assumed to characterise the current maintained releases.

A different axis of generality is pursued by pathway-level integration tools. The pathwayMultiomics package provides a roll-up strategy that does not require matched samples and uses a novel MiniMax statistic to prioritise dysregulated pathways across categorical, continuous or survival outcomes [R32]. By aggregating features before integration, such methods trade the resolution of gene-level signals for robustness and interpretability; the available excerpt does not address how pathwayMultiomics handles the compositional structure that dominates microbiome data, where correlation networks at the pathway level can be driven by shared denominators rather than shared biology, so its applicability to compositional microbiome inputs should be regarded as untested rather than unsupported.

A fourth layer consists of wrapper pipelines that treat the proliferation of integration methods as a usability problem rather than a statistical one. moiraine automates preprocessing, input formatting, visualisation and side-by-side comparison of several integration tools on the same dataset [R7], while MUUMI unifies statistical meta-analysis with network-based integration, including similarity network fusion, to identify robust molecular signatures in IPF transcriptomic and macrophage multi-omics data [R6]. Neither wrapper ships with a Bayesian assessment of whether one integrated solution is genuinely better than another; they make comparison easier but do not adjudicate it. Similarly, SUMO provides controlled synthetic multi-omics data with user-defined latent structures [R11], yet the absence of a broadly adopted ground-truth corpus continues to limit head-to-head evaluation of competing methods on a level methodological playing field.

Taken together, the generalist frameworks provide a coordinated data infrastructure [R36, R51], two dominant inferential families with distinct theoretical foundations (PLS-based [R3, R35] and Bayesian factor-analytic [R2, R4]), and an emerging layer of comparison tooling and simulation infrastructure [R7, R6, R11]. What the present evidence does not establish is that any of these general-purpose stacks ship, by default, with the microbiome-specific preparation logic that dedicated microbiome workflows typically require; this gap is part of the motivation behind microbiome-flavoured workflows such as EasyMultiProfiler, which build on the same MultiAssayExperiment container and provide a module-oriented R interface (extraction, preparation, support, analysis, visualisation), illustrated on human and mouse gut host–microbiome datasets [R1]. The same caveat about absent head-to-head benchmarking applies symmetrically to the comparison frameworks discussed above [R7, R6, R11], and to the as-yet-unstated behaviour of MOFA-family factor models on microbiome inputs [R2, R4, R42].
